screens.title: What is DNS and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: DNS, the Domain Name System, is a hierarchical naming system that translates human-friendly domain names into machine addresses. Put simply, it lets you use example. com instead of remembering numbers like 192.0.2.1. In cloud architectures DNS does more than browsing: it supports service discovery between microservices, lets load balancers present stable names while backend IPs change, and underpins disaster-recovery patterns by directing traffic to healthy endpoints. A concrete example: you register mydomain. com, create A records for web servers, and point an Alias to an Application Load Balancer so users reach your service even when instances change. A common misconception is thinking DNS is a one-time configuration. DNS records and routing policies are active elements of architecture that must be designed for updates, TTL behavior, and failover. Another contrast: the zone apex cannot be a CNAME if you have other records there; use an Alias record instead. When designing, think about TTLs and how quickly clients will see changes, pair health checks with failover to avoid sending traffic to unhealthy hosts, and use private hosted zones when you want names to resolve only within a VPC. How will you balance TTL length with your need to redirect traffic during an outage?

keyIdea.text: DNS maps names to addresses; in cloud systems it enables discovery, load distribution, and failover.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What is DNS and why it matters
Definition
DNS is a hierarchical and decentralized naming system that maps domain names to IP addresses and other resources.
Key points
  • Enables human-readable names for services and hosts.
  • Supports service discovery, load distribution, and failover.
  • TTL controls how long clients cache DNS responses.
Concrete example
Register mydomain.com, create A records for two web servers, and use a load balancer alias to present a stable endpoint even as instances change.
Common misconception
DNS is not static configuration; record choices and TTLs affect availability and update behavior.
Key Takeaway

Treat DNS as an active routing layer: plan record types, TTLs, and health checks to meet availability goals.

Analogy
Think of DNS as a phonebook: names map to numbers, but in the cloud the phonebook can point to a load balancer that reorganizes calls behind the scenes.
Why this matters in AWS
Route 53 integrates name resolution with AWS resources and health checks so DNS can actively improve resilience without manual IP updates.
Check your understanding
If a service must remain reachable even when an instance fails, which DNS features will you combine to achieve that?

screens.title: Amazon Route 53 — capabilities and role
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Route 53 is AWS’s managed DNS service that combines domain registration, DNS routing, and health checks into a globally distributed system. It assigns name servers for hosted zones and can route queries to AWS resources such as EC2 instances, Elastic Load Balancers, S3 static websites, or to external endpoints. A concrete example: you register mydomain. com, create a public hosted zone in Route 53, then create an Alias record that references your Application Load Balancer so the root domain resolves correctly and updates automatically as the ALB changes. Route 53 health checks continuously probe endpoints and feed into failover routing so traffic is sent only to healthy targets. A common misconception is treating Route 53 as only a registrar; in practice it is a routing platform with integrated monitoring. When designing systems, consider how Route 53 interacts with other AWS components: Alias records simplify apex mapping, and global routing policies help you reduce latency and meet regional compliance requirements. As you learn, focus on how registration, routing, and health checks form a triad that keeps names accurate and services reachable.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Amazon Route 53 — capabilities and role
Core services
Domain Registration
Register or transfer domains and manage name servers.
DNS Routing
Create hosted zones and record sets that map names to resources.
Health Checks
Monitor endpoints and integrate with failover routing to protect availability.
Concrete example
Create a public hosted zone for mydomain.com, add an Alias to an ALB so the apex resolves correctly, and attach health checks for failover records so traffic shifts automatically when an endpoint is down.
Common pitfall
Assuming Route 53 is only a registrar. In reality it is a global routing service integrated with AWS resources and monitoring.
Key Takeaway

Route 53 is more than registration: use its routing and health checks to design resilient name resolution tied to AWS resources.

screens.title: Hosted Zones: Public vs Private
screens.narratorSegment: Hosted zones are containers for DNS records for a domain and its subdomains. Public hosted zones make records internet-routable: when you register a domain in Route 53 or transfer it, you create a public hosted zone and Route 53 assigns four authoritative name servers to publish. Public zones are appropriate for websites and services that must be reachable by external users. Private hosted zones, by contrast, are scoped to one or more VPCs and resolve only within those VPCs. Use a private hosted zone when you want internal names like api. internal. example. com to map to private IPs without exposing them publicly. A concrete example: deploy an internal microservice and create a private hosted zone associated with your VPC; internal instances resolve service. example. com to a private IP while the name is unseen on the internet. A common mistake is creating a public zone for internal-only services — that exposes names and can cause routing leaks. When designing, consider which records must be internet-visible and which must remain VPC-local, and associate private zones with every VPC that needs access.

keyIdea.title: Hosted zone choice
keyIdea.text: Public zones for internet-facing names; private zones for VPC-internal resolution and service discovery.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Hosted Zones: Public vs Private
Public Hosted Zone
Used to route traffic on the internet. Route 53 assigns four name servers and the domain registrar points to them.
When to use
  • Websites, APIs, and any internet-routable service.
  • When users outside your VPC must resolve the domain.
Private Hosted Zone
Used to route traffic within one or more VPCs. Records resolve to private IPs and are not available on the public internet.
When to use
  • Internal services, microservices, and databases accessible only from VPCs.
  • Service discovery for internal applications.
Example
api.internal.example.com in a private hosted zone resolves to a private IP inside the VPC.
Common mistake
Creating a public hosted zone for an internal-only service, which exposes DNS records publicly.
Check
Associate private hosted zones only with the VPCs that need the records.

screens.title: Route 53 Record Types
screens.narratorSegment: Record sets map names to addresses or other resources. Route 53 supports common DNS record types and a few AWS-specific extensions. An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address; AAAA maps to an IPv6 address. A CNAME maps one domain name to another, useful for aliasing subdomains, but it cannot be used at the zone apex when other records exist. Route 53 introduces Alias records, which look like CNAME behavior but can point to AWS resources and are allowed at the apex; they also update automatically and have no extra cost. MX records direct mail to mail servers, NS records list the authoritative name servers for a zone, and SOA holds administrative info like the primary name server and contact. TXT records carry arbitrary text for verification or SPF rules. SRV records locate services with protocol and port data. A common misconception is thinking Alias records behave exactly like CNAMEs; Alias integrates with AWS services and can be used at the apex, while CNAME cannot. When designing records, align type to purpose: address mapping, mail routing, service discovery, or AWS resource aliasing.

keyIdea.title: Record selection
keyIdea.text: Use A/AAAA for addresses, CNAME for name-to-name (not at apex), Alias for AWS resources at apex, and MX/NS/SOA/TXT/SRV for specialized roles.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Route 53 Record Types
A / AAAA
A maps to IPv4; AAAA maps to IPv6 addresses for direct host resolution.
CNAME
Maps a name to another name. Not permitted at the zone apex when other records exist.
Alias
Route 53 extension that points to AWS resources and can be used at the zone apex; updates automatically.
MX / NS / SOA
MX for mail servers, NS lists name servers, SOA stores authoritative domain metadata.
TXT / SRV
TXT for verification and SPF; SRV locates named services with ports and priorities.
Key Takeaway

Match record types to intent: address mapping, name aliasing, mail routing, or AWS-resource aliasing at the apex.

screens.title: Alias records versus CNAME and apex rules
screens.narratorSegment: Alias records in Route 53 emulate CNAME behavior but with important differences that matter for cloud architectures. Use a CNAME when you need one name to resolve to another name for a subdomain, such as www. example. com to example. com. However, a CNAME cannot be placed at the zone apex if other records (like NS or SOA) exist. Alias records let you point the zone apex to AWS resources such as an Application Load Balancer, CloudFront distribution, or S3 website. They are free and update automatically as the underlying resource changes. A concrete example: you want example. com to resolve to an ALB. Creating a CNAME at the apex would be invalid; instead create an Alias record that references the ALB. A common misconception is thinking Alias records are identical to CNAMEs; Alias integrates with AWS targets, supports apex placement, and behaves differently in billing and DNS resolution. When planning, use Alias for AWS targets and apex resolution, and reserve CNAME for mapping one non-apex name to another when needed. Alias records versus CNAME and apex rules means use alias records for aws resources and apex mapping; cname for subdomain-to-name mapping where apex rules don't apply.. In practical terms, when to use alias records instead of cnames. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use Alias records for AWS resources and apex mapping; CNAME for subdomain-to-name mapping where apex rules don't apply.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Alias records versus CNAME and apex rules
When to use CNAME
Map a subdomain to another domain name, such as blog.example.com → host.provider.com.
Limit
Cannot be used at zone apex when other records exist.
When to use Alias
Point a name to an AWS resource and place it at the zone apex; updates automatically and has no charge per DNS query.
Advantage
Use Alias to connect example.com to an ALB or CloudFront distribution safely.
Example
Use Alias to point example.com to an ALB; CNAME works for www.example.com to example.com only if not at apex.
Pitfall
Attempting a CNAME at the apex will create an invalid configuration if NS or SOA records exist.
Takeaway
Prefer Alias for AWS targets and apex mapping; use CNAME for non-apex aliasing between names.

screens.title: Routing Policies overview
screens.narratorSegment: Routing policies determine how Route 53 answers DNS queries and where users end up. Simple routing sends all queries to a single resource. Weighted routing distributes traffic across resources according to weights you assign, useful for A/B testing or gradual deployments. Latency-based routing sends users to the region with the lowest measured latency, which requires deploying resources in multiple regions. Geolocation routing considers the user’s geographic origin and maps them to specific resources, and geoproximity lets you bias routing toward or away from certain resources. Failover routing requires paired primary and secondary records with health checks; Route 53 sends traffic to the secondary only when the primary is unhealthy. Multivalue answer routing returns up to eight healthy records at random, giving clients multiple resolution options without being a load balancer. A common misconception is expecting DNS to evenly load-balance clients like a load balancer; DNS-based routing distributes resolution choices but is not equivalent to connection-level load balancing. When selecting a policy, match it to the goal: performance, directed regional traffic, gradual rollout, or high-availability failover. Routing Policies overview means choose routing policies to meet goals: simple, weighted, latency, geolocation, geoproximity, failover, or multivalue answer.. In practical terms, how route 53 chooses which resource answers a query. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Choose routing policies to meet goals: simple, weighted, latency, geolocation, geoproximity, failover, or multivalue Answer.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Routing Policies overview
Simple
One resource answers all queries; no health checks required.
Weighted
Distribute traffic by weight for A/B tests or staged rollouts.
Latency
Send users to the AWS region with the lowest latency.
Geolocation
Route users based on their geographic origin to region-specific endpoints.
Geoproximity
Bias routing based on proximity and optional traffic weighting to resources.
Failover & Multivalue
Failover uses health checks for primary/secondary; multivalue returns multiple healthy records to clients.
Quick decision guide
Choose weighted for staged rollouts, latency for performance across regions, geolocation for regional compliance, and failover with health checks for high availability.

screens.title: Weighted routing — staged rollouts and A/B testing
screens.narratorSegment: Weighted routing lets you split DNS traffic across multiple resources by assigning weights. It’s handy for A/B testing, canary releases, or gradual rollouts when you want to limit exposure to a new version. For example, if you have two endpoints and want 90% of traffic to remain on the stable version and 10% to go to a new release, assign weights that reflect that ratio. Route 53 returns records according to the defined weights when clients resolve the name. One subtle misconception is assuming weighted routing performs session-aware load balancing; DNS-based weights only influence name resolution and clients may cache the answer according to TTL, so connection-level balancing still depends on the target infrastructure. When using weighted routing, set suitable TTLs to control how long clients cache the DNS answer and plan for gradual weight changes to observe behavior. Also test with representative clients to validate that error rates and performance meet expectations before increasing weight. What weight would you assign if you wanted a safe 5% canary rollout? content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Weighted routing — staged rollouts and A/B testing
How it works
  1. Create multiple records with the same name and record type.
  2. Assign a numeric weight to each record to control relative distribution.
  3. Route 53 returns answers in proportion to weights when clients resolve the name.
Example
Primary weight 90, canary weight 10 yields roughly 10% of DNS resolutions pointing to the canary endpoint, subject to TTL and client caching.
Misconception
DNS weights are not connection-level load balancing. They affect resolution choices; session persistence and client behavior determine traffic persistence.
Key Takeaway

Use weighted routing for controlled rollouts, set short TTLs for quicker shifts, and monitor client behavior to validate the distribution.

screens.title: Latency and Geolocation routing
screens.narratorSegment: Latency-based routing and geolocation routing solve different problems. Use latency routing to send users to the AWS region that gives the lowest network latency; this requires deploying identical resources in multiple regions so the routing decision has a performance benefit. A concrete example: users in Europe are routed to a Frankfurt region endpoint because it reports lower latency than a Singapore region. Geolocation routing, by contrast, maps users based on their location to specific resources and can enforce regional compliance or local content delivery. Geoproximity allows biasing traffic toward resources by adjusting a bias value that shifts the geographic boundaries. A common misconception is using geolocation when latency routing would better improve user-perceived speed. Also, geolocation and geoproximity can interact with regulatory or data residency needs; choose geolocation when you must return traffic to a specific country or continent. When designing, document which policy meets your performance, legal, and operational goals and ensure resources exist in the referenced regions before applying the policy. Latency-based Routing
Routes users to the region with the lowest latency. Requires identical resources in multiple regions.
When to use
When user-perceived latency is the priority and multi-region deployment is available.
Geolocation & Geoproximity
Geolocation routes by user location; geoproximity biases by distance and optional traffic shift values.
When to use
When regional compliance or content localization is required, or when biasing traffic helps balance load geographically.

screens.title: Failover routing and health checks
screens.narratorSegment: Failover routing pairs primary and secondary records and relies on Route 53 Health Checks to decide when to switch traffic. Health checks probe endpoints—HTTP, TCP, or other supported types—so Route 53 knows whether an endpoint is healthy. A practical step-by-step example from the chapter: create two EC2 web servers, assign public IPs such as 54.1.1.1 for Primary and 54.2.2.2 for Secondary, then create health checks that probe /index. html on port 80 for each. In your hosted zone create two A records with the same name and set routing policy to Failover, marking one as Primary and the other as Secondary, associating each with its corresponding health check. When the Primary becomes unhealthy, Route 53 will stop returning it and will answer with the Secondary. A common pitfall is misconfiguring health check endpoints or paths, which can mark healthy resources as unhealthy. Always test failover by stopping the web service on the primary host—using commands like sudo systemctl stop httpd or sudo systemctl stop nginx—and observe DNS resolution and the site returning the secondary content. After recovery, Route 53 will return traffic to the primary when health checks pass again.

fullNarratorScript:
DNS is the phonebook of the internet: it maps human-friendly names to machine addresses so users and services can find each other. In cloud architectures DNS becomes a core building block for service discovery, availability, load distribution, and disaster recovery. In this chapter you will learn what hosted zones are, how Route 53 record types map names to addresses or AWS resources, and how routing policies let you control traffic flow globally. You will also practice setting up health checks and a failover policy to keep a simple website available when one server fails. A working understanding of Route 53 helps you design resilient systems: use public hosted zones for internet-facing domains, private hosted zones for internal resolution inside VPCs, and Alias records when you must point the zone apex to AWS resources like load balancers. As you move through the lesson, notice common pitfalls — for example, trying to use a CNAME at the zone apex — and learn the practical pattern: use Alias at the apex and pair failover with health checks. By the end, you’ll be able to choose record types and routing policies that match availability and performance requirements.

These objectives map directly to practical skills you will use when designing DNS for cloud systems. First, you will explain DNS fundamentals: what it means to resolve a domain name to an IP address and why DNS underpins service discovery and availability. Second, you will describe what Route 53 offers: registration, DNS routing, Alias records, and health checks that enable automatic failover. Third, you will create and manage hosted zones — both public zones for internet-facing domains and private zones for VPC-local names — and understand why private zones keep internal services private. Finally, you will distinguish record types and choose the right one: for instance, use A for IPv4 addresses, AAAA for IPv6, CNAME for mapping one name to another, and Alias to point the zone apex to an ELB. Each objective prepares you to make architecture decisions that improve reliability and maintainability.

This second objectives panel focuses on applied tasks and decisions you'll practice in the lab. You will learn to implement routing policies such as simple, weighted, latency, geolocation, and failover. That includes assigning weights for gradual rollouts and using latency routing to send users to the lowest-latency region. You will configure Route 53 Health Checks and use them with failover records so traffic moves automatically when an endpoint becomes unhealthy. You will also practice using Alias records when pointing the zone apex to AWS resources like an ALB; this avoids invalid CNAME-at-apex configurations. Finally, you will test your configuration using simple network tools and simulate a failure to see failover in action. These objectives ensure you can both design and validate DNS behavior for resilient applications. Learning Objectives — Applied Skills means practice routing policies, health checks, alias usage, and testing to validate resilient dns configurations.. In practical terms, hands-on capabilities and policy choices you'll practice. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

DNS, the Domain Name System, is a hierarchical naming system that translates human-friendly domain names into machine addresses. Put simply, it lets you use example. com instead of remembering numbers like 192.0.2.1. In cloud architectures DNS does more than browsing: it supports service discovery between microservices, lets load balancers present stable names while backend IPs change, and underpins disaster-recovery patterns by directing traffic to healthy endpoints. A concrete example: you register mydomain. com, create A records for web servers, and point an Alias to an Application Load Balancer so users reach your service even when instances change. A common misconception is thinking DNS is a one-time configuration. DNS records and routing policies are active elements of architecture that must be designed for updates, TTL behavior, and failover. Another contrast: the zone apex cannot be a CNAME if you have other records there; use an Alias record instead. When designing, think about TTLs and how quickly clients will see changes, pair health checks with failover to avoid sending traffic to unhealthy hosts, and use private hosted zones when you want names to resolve only within a VPC. How will you balance TTL length with your need to redirect traffic during an outage?

Amazon Route 53 is AWS’s managed DNS service that combines domain registration, DNS routing, and health checks into a globally distributed system. It assigns name servers for hosted zones and can route queries to AWS resources such as EC2 instances, Elastic Load Balancers, S3 static websites, or to external endpoints. A concrete example: you register mydomain. com, create a public hosted zone in Route 53, then create an Alias record that references your Application Load Balancer so the root domain resolves correctly and updates automatically as the ALB changes. Route 53 health checks continuously probe endpoints and feed into failover routing so traffic is sent only to healthy targets. A common misconception is treating Route 53 as only a registrar; in practice it is a routing platform with integrated monitoring. When designing systems, consider how Route 53 interacts with other AWS components: Alias records simplify apex mapping, and global routing policies help you reduce latency and meet regional compliance requirements. As you learn, focus on how registration, routing, and health checks form a triad that keeps names accurate and services reachable.

Hosted zones are containers for DNS records for a domain and its subdomains. Public hosted zones make records internet-routable: when you register a domain in Route 53 or transfer it, you create a public hosted zone and Route 53 assigns four authoritative name servers to publish. Public zones are appropriate for websites and services that must be reachable by external users. Private hosted zones, by contrast, are scoped to one or more VPCs and resolve only within those VPCs. Use a private hosted zone when you want internal names like api. internal. example. com to map to private IPs without exposing them publicly. A concrete example: deploy an internal microservice and create a private hosted zone associated with your VPC; internal instances resolve service. example. com to a private IP while the name is unseen on the internet. A common mistake is creating a public zone for internal-only services — that exposes names and can cause routing leaks. When designing, consider which records must be internet-visible and which must remain VPC-local, and associate private zones with every VPC that needs access.

Record sets map names to addresses or other resources. Route 53 supports common DNS record types and a few AWS-specific extensions. An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address; AAAA maps to an IPv6 address. A CNAME maps one domain name to another, useful for aliasing subdomains, but it cannot be used at the zone apex when other records exist. Route 53 introduces Alias records, which look like CNAME behavior but can point to AWS resources and are allowed at the apex; they also update automatically and have no extra cost. MX records direct mail to mail servers, NS records list the authoritative name servers for a zone, and SOA holds administrative info like the primary name server and contact. TXT records carry arbitrary text for verification or SPF rules. SRV records locate services with protocol and port data. A common misconception is thinking Alias records behave exactly like CNAMEs; Alias integrates with AWS services and can be used at the apex, while CNAME cannot. When designing records, align type to purpose: address mapping, mail routing, service discovery, or AWS resource aliasing.

Alias records in Route 53 emulate CNAME behavior but with important differences that matter for cloud architectures. Use a CNAME when you need one name to resolve to another name for a subdomain, such as www. example. com to example. com. However, a CNAME cannot be placed at the zone apex if other records (like NS or SOA) exist. Alias records let you point the zone apex to AWS resources such as an Application Load Balancer, CloudFront distribution, or S3 website. They are free and update automatically as the underlying resource changes. A concrete example: you want example. com to resolve to an ALB. Creating a CNAME at the apex would be invalid; instead create an Alias record that references the ALB. A common misconception is thinking Alias records are identical to CNAMEs; Alias integrates with AWS targets, supports apex placement, and behaves differently in billing and DNS resolution. When planning, use Alias for AWS targets and apex resolution, and reserve CNAME for mapping one non-apex name to another when needed. Alias records versus CNAME and apex rules means use alias records for aws resources and apex mapping; cname for subdomain-to-name mapping where apex rules don't apply.. In practical terms, when to use alias records instead of cnames. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A common pitfall is misconfiguring health check endpoints or paths, which can mark healthy resources as unhealthy. Use A and AAAA for direct IP mappings; CNAME for name-to-name aliasing on subdomains; Alias for AWS resources and apex mapping.
